issues.legal_issue: A party must appeal every adverse decree in connected suits tried on common issues, because an unappealed decree may become res judicata in an appeal concerning another connected suit.
material_facts: Three related suits were decided by separate decrees under a common judgment after common issues were framed and common evidence was recorded.
The tenants appealed the decree in only one of the suits, leaving adverse decrees in the other suits unchallenged.
The disputes in the suits shared the question of the character and transferability of the property, which the tenants had raised in their pleadings.
issues.conclusion: The unappealed decrees attained finality and operated as res judicata against the tenants in the appeal from the connected suit; the tenants’ challenge was foreclosed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC applies where a matter directly and substantially in issue between the same parties has been heard and finally decided in a former suit. Under Explanation I, a suit is former when decided earlier, regardless of when it was instituted. Where connected suits have common issues and a common trial but separate adverse decrees, the losing party must appeal the adverse decrees; a decree not appealed becomes final and may bar relitigation. This follows Lonankutty v. Thomman, Narayana Prabhu Venkateswara Prabhu v. Narayana Prabhu Krishna Prabhu, Premier Tyres Ltd. v. Kerala State Road Transport Corporation, and Sheodan Singh v. Daryao Kunwar. Where suits have specifically been consolidated, filing a single appeal may put the entire dispute back in issue, as recognized in Chitivalasa Jute Mills v. Jaypee Rewa Cement.

rule.if: connected_suits_appeal and common_issues_decided and common_trial_held and separate_adverse_decrees and decree_left_unappealed

predicates.connected_suits_appeal: A party appeals a decree arising from one of several connected suits.
predicates.common_issues_decided: The connected suits involve issues that are common or substantially similar.
predicates.common_trial_held: The court tried the connected suits together and considered common evidence.
predicates.separate_adverse_decrees: The court entered separate decrees that were adverse to the same party.
predicates.decree_left_unappealed: The party did not appeal one or more of those adverse decrees.
predicates.unappealed_decree_bars_relitigation: An adverse decree left unappealed prevents the party from relitigating the matter it finally decided.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns one of several connected suits tried on common issues, and a separate adverse decree in another such suit is left unappealed, that decree bars relitigation of the matter it decided.

issues.legal_issue: A party that pleads a challenge to a property transfer in its first suit must seek the corresponding relief in that suit and cannot reserve the challenge for later litigation.
material_facts: In a suit seeking recognition of leasehold rights and protection of possession, the tenants pleaded that the transfer of the property was invalid and that the transferees had no title.

Although the prayer was awkwardly worded and did not expressly seek a separate declaration concerning title, the court found that the pleading and first prayer showed an intention to challenge the transfer.
The tenants sought to raise the transfer and title dispute in later proceedings without appealing the dismissal of the first suit.
issues.conclusion: Order II Rule 2 CPC barred the tenants from reserving the pleaded challenge to the transfer for a later proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Order II Rule 2 CPC bars a later suit for relief arising from a cause of action when the plaintiff omitted to claim that relief in the earlier suit, subject to the rule’s requirements. The court held that the pleadings and prayer, read in substance, showed that the tenants sought to assail the transfer; the bar would not apply if they had merely alleged an apprehension of dispossession without challenging the property’s legal character or the transferor’s capacity to convey it.

predicates.first_suit_seeks_possession_protection: A plaintiff brings a first suit seeking recognition of a right to possess property or protection against interference with possession.
predicates.transfer_challenge_pleaded: The plaintiff’s pleadings challenge the validity of a transfer or the transferor’s capacity to make it.
predicates.related_transfer_relief_omitted: The plaintiff does not seek the relief corresponding to that pleaded transfer challenge in the first suit.
predicates.omitted_transfer_relief_barred_later: The plaintiff cannot pursue the omitted transfer-related relief in a later proceeding.

issues.definition: When a first suit seeks protection of possession and pleads a challenge to a transfer but omits the corresponding relief, the plaintiff cannot pursue that relief later.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot, during the tenancy, deny that the landlord who put the tenant in possession had title to the property when the tenancy began.
material_facts: The tenants entered possession under leases granted by the original landlord, and a succeeding lease was made between the tenants and the trust through its representative.
The trust’s rent claim concerned a period before it transferred the property to the transferees.
The tenants challenged the trust’s ownership in resisting that claim.
issues.conclusion: The tenants were precluded from challenging the title of the landlord who had put them in possession; the court noted that the position could differ in a dispute between the tenants and the transferees.
issues.legal_principle: Section 116 of the Evidence Act provides that, during a tenancy, a tenant or a person claiming through the tenant cannot deny that the landlord had title to the immovable property at the beginning of the tenancy. The court applied that estoppel to a dispute concerning rent claimed by the original landlord for a period before the transfer, while distinguishing a dispute between the tenants and the transferees.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_proceeding and landlord_put_tenant_in_possession and tenancy_continues and tenant_challenges_original_landlord_title

predicates.landlord_tenant_proceeding: The dispute is between a landlord and a tenant concerning their tenancy.
predicates.landlord_put_tenant_in_possession: The landlord placed the tenant in possession of the property under the tenancy.
predicates.tenancy_continues: The tenancy under which the tenant entered possession is continuing.
predicates.tenant_challenges_original_landlord_titl: The tenant disputes the title held by the landlord who placed the tenant in possession when the tenancy began.
predicates.tenant_cannot_deny_original_landlord_tit: The tenant is precluded from denying that the original landlord had title when the tenancy began.

issues.definition: During a continuing tenancy, a tenant whom the landlord placed in possession cannot deny that landlord’s title at the beginning of the tenancy.
